title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. Problem 3 (§30) asks for a curve y(x) taking prescribed values p, q, r, ... at the equally spaced abscissae x = nθ, (n+1)θ, ... . Write x = θω. Euler treats y/ω as a function of ω² and builds an infinite Lagrange-type interpolant on the nodes ω² = (n+k)²:

y/ω = Σ_k ± (p_k/(n+k)) Π_{j≠k} ((n+j)² − ω²)/((n+j)² − (n+k)²).

The leading infinite product is 𝔄 = Π_{j≥1} (n+j−ω)(n+j+ω)/(j(2n+j)) = Γ(2n+1)/(Γ(n+1−ω)Γ(n+1+ω)). Euler writes 𝔄 = 2/((n−ω)Δ). The other coefficients are rational multiples of 𝔄. The interpolant is then

nΔy/(2(n+ω)ω) = Σ_k (−1)^k ((2n)_k/k!) p_k/((n+k)² − ω²).

This page.
- Opening lines of the page. At a node ω = n+k one denominator vanishes, Δ also becomes infinite, and the formula returns y = p_k.
- Cor. 1 (§31). Take p_k = sin(n+k)θ, expecting y = sin ωθ. This gives the three-parameter (n, θ, ω) identity
  nΔ sin ωθ/(2(n+ω)ω) = Σ_k (−1)^k (2n)_k/k! · sin((n+k)θ)/((n+k)² − ω²).
- Cor. 2 (§32). With θ = π every sin(n+k)π = (−1)^k sin nπ, so the series becomes Σ (2n)_k/k! · 1/((n+k)² − ω²).
  - For n = 1/2 all binomial weights equal 1. The series is Σ 4/((2k+1)² − 4ω²) = (π/(2ω)) tan ωπ, a sum Euler already had.
  - Hence Δ = (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ.
  - Euler identifies Δ with a Beta integral, printed as ∫ z^{−ω−1/2}(1−z)^{−ω−1/2} dz = 2∫ z^{1/2−ω}(1−z)^{−1/2−ω} dz.
- Scholion 1 (§33). Euler warns that the interpolating curve need not be the sine curve, since infinitely many curves pass through the same points. He begins writing the general solution y = Θ + f(Ω), where Ω vanishes at every node. On the next page Ω = 2ω(n+ω)/Δ, and Euler says agreement with sin ωθ may depend on θ and n.

Modern check.
- Δ = 2Γ(n−ω)Γ(n+1+ω)/Γ(2n+1) = 2B(n−ω, n+1+ω).
- Cor. 2 becomes Σ_k (2n)_k/k! · 1/((n+k)² − ω²) = nΓ(n−ω)Γ(n+ω) sin πω/(ωΓ(2n+1) sin nπ).
  - The residues at ω = ±(n+k) match: both sides give −(2n)_k/(2k!(n+k)).
  - Both sides decay for 0 < n < 1, so the identity is exactly true there. It is a Mittag-Leffler expansion of Γ(n−ω)Γ(n+ω) sin πω/ω.
- For n = 1/2, Cor. 1 is the classical half-integer Fourier expansion π sin ωθ/(2ω cos ωπ) = Σ (−1)^k sin((k+½)θ)/((k+½)² − ω²), valid for |θ| ≤ π.
- For general n, Cor. 1 is a non-orthogonal expansion of sin ωθ in the functions sin(n+k)θ.
- Ω has exponential type π in ω, and sin ωθ/ω has type |θ|. By a Carlson-type uniqueness argument the interpolant reproduces sin ωθ when |θ| < π (θ = π also works, as shown above).
- For |θ| > π it generally fails. Shifting θ by 2π reproduces the node values only up to the factor e^{2πin}, so the series cannot equal sin ωθ for all θ unless n is an integer.
- So Euler's suspicion that validity depends on θ and n is correct, and the precise answer is |θ| ≤ π.
errors: The Beta-integral expression for Δ is wrong. It descends from the previous page's formula Δ = ∫ z^{n−ω−1}(1−z)^{n−ω−1} dz = B(n−ω, n−ω).
The value consistent with 𝔄 = 2/((n−ω)Δ) is Δ = 2∫_0^1 z^{n−ω−1}(1−z)^{n+ω} dz = 2Γ(n−ω)Γ(n+1+ω)/Γ(2n+1).

For n = 1/2 the two printed forms ∫ z^{−ω−1/2}(1−z)^{−ω−1/2} dz and 2∫ z^{1/2−ω}(1−z)^{−1/2−ω} dz agree with each other (both equal B(1/2−ω, 1/2−ω)). Neither equals the correct Δ = 2Γ(1/2−ω)Γ(3/2+ω) = (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ, except at ω = 0. At ω = 1/4 the printed integral gives about 7.42, against about 6.66 for the closed form.
In the second printed form the exponent of z should be 1/2+ω, not 1/2−ω.
Euler's final closed form Δ = (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ is nevertheless correct for Δ as defined through 𝔄. The equation Δ = closed form = printed integral is false.

Consequence for the next page (§34): Euler's discussion of a possible correction term Φ and his ω→0 argument rest on the false integral. In fact Φ ≡ 0 for θ = π, n = 1/2, and the ω→0 argument would not establish this in any case.

Convergence: the interpolation series converge only for n < 1, since the terms behave like k^{2n−3} times bounded factors. Euler states no restriction, although he says n, θ, ω may be chosen freely (pro lubitu).

ideas.what: Infinite Lagrange/Newton interpolation in ω² through nodes (n+k)², with an infinite-product (Gamma/Beta) normaliser Δ
ideas.modern_name: infinite Lagrange interpolation / cardinal-type series with Gamma-function node polynomial
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (infinite interpolation); later Whittaker, Nörlund, Carlson
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula analytica I, 1783); related interpolation work in E613 and others (unsure of exact list)

ideas.what: Three-parameter identity expanding sin ωθ in sin((n+k)θ) with weights (2n)_k/k! over (n+k)² − ω²
ideas.modern_name: non-orthogonal sine-series expansion / interpolation series of an entire function of exponential type
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure; the n = 1/2 case is the classical Fourier expansion (Euler, Fourier)

ideas.what: Partial-fraction sum Σ (2n)_k/k! · 1/((n+k)² − ω²) = nΓ(n−ω)Γ(n+ω) sin πω/(ωΓ(2n+1) sin nπ), valid for 0<n<1
ideas.modern_name: Mittag-Leffler expansion of a Gamma/Beta product (hypergeometric partial fractions)
ideas.where_published: E555 §32, implicit (Euler leaves Δ as an integral)
Introductio in analysin infinitorum (E101), ch. X

ideas.what: Non-uniqueness of interpolation: general solution Θ + f(Ω), with Ω vanishing at every node; doubt whether the interpolant equals sin ωθ depending on θ and n
ideas.modern_name: uniqueness of interpolation of entire functions (Carlson's theorem, exponential type < π)
ideas.where_published: E555 §33–34; Euler raises similar caveats elsewhere (unsure where)

missed.claim: Euler asks for which θ and n the interpolant Θ coincides with sin ωθ and leaves the question open. The answer, via Carlson-type growth theory, is |θ| ≤ π for 0<n<1. It fails generally for |θ| > π because of the 2π-shift factor e^{2πin}. This is a precise early formulation of the exponential-type condition for uniqueness of interpolation.
missed.quote: Fieri vero posset, vt pro aliis abscissis, vbi i non est numerus integer, ideoque generatim si x=ωθ, non foret applicata y=sin.ωθ.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A specific 18th-century instance of the Carlson/cardinal-series uniqueness problem. Histories of sampling theory and interpolation (e.g. Butzer and collaborators) may not cite this passage.

missed.claim: The general-n identity of Cor. 1, a binomially weighted expansion of sin ωθ in sin(n+k)θ, appears to be a non-classical expansion. Its θ=π specialisation is an exact Gamma-function partial-fraction formula.
missed.quote: vbi imprimis notatu est dignum, quod tres litterae, n, θ et ω, pro lubitu accipi queant.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A minor but explicit closed-form family. Probably derivable from standard hypergeometric identities, so novelty is limited; unsure whether it is catalogued.

missed.claim: The printed Beta integral for Δ is wrong; the correct one is 2B(n−ω, n+1+ω). Euler's closed form (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ is right, but his equating it to the printed integral is false. The Φ-argument of §34 is therefore built on an error.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A correction for editors and commentators of E555. Unsure whether the Opera omnia notes flag it.

deep.surprise_reason: Mostly a correct application of Euler's infinite interpolation, with a well-known tangent sum. The modestly notable points are an explicit, correct concern about non-uniqueness that anticipates Carlson's theorem, an unusual three-parameter sine expansion, and an uncorrected Beta-integral error that undermines the following scholion.
transcription_corrections: Machine transcription of the integral forms appears faithful to the print. The print itself carries the error: mathematically the exponent should be z^{1/2+ω}, i.e. Δ = 2∫ z^{n−ω−1}(1−z)^{n+ω} dz in general.
In Cor. 2 the denominators read (n+1)² − ω², (n+2)² − ω², etc., and for n = 1/2 the series reads 4/(1−4ω²) + 4/(9−4ω²) + 4/(25−4ω²) + ...; the transcription is consistent with this.
